what_this_is: Answer-level log for the printed competency booklets. Scoped to the question banks below: questions are asked ONLY from here, never invented. Separate from the repo-root progress.json, which logs concepts taught in conversation.
how_it_runs: On demand only. No schedule. The learner says they want questions; a session reads this file and picks.
Pick order: untested first, then shaky, then comfortable items whose last_attempted is over 35 days old (stale, not failed). Never two in a row from the same part.
Ask ONE question, verbatim from 'prompt'. Withhold the ideal answer.
Grade per .claude/skills/learn/references/house-style.md -> 'Record the gap'. File the verbatim attempt per .claude/skills/track/SKILL.md -> 'Graded attempts'.
Update the question row and the competency rollup, then commit.

status_rules.shaky: attempted, and either the last verdict was not a pass or the pass streak is under 2
status_rules.stale: not a stored status - derived at read time: comfortable, but last_attempted is more than 35 days ago. Unverified, not failed. Say so honestly rather than demoting it.

miss_codes.name: didn't produce the term - go back to the term table
miss_codes.mechanism: named it, got the causality or direction wrong - go back to the anchor sketch
miss_codes.boundary: confused it with its look-alike - go back to the boundary column
miss_codes.price: prescribed without naming the cost - go back to the trade-offs table
miss_codes.phrasing: had it, couldn't say it in expert terms - go back to the plain/expert table

competencies.title: Stability Antipatterns & Stability Patterns
competencies.answer_key: resources/release-it-ch4-5/booklet.html — section 9, frozen before any attempt

questions.prompt: Your payments service calls an external fraud-scoring API. During an incident, monitoring shows CPU at 3%, memory flat, no errors in the application log — and yet every request-handling thread is occupied and the service returns nothing to anyone. (a) Name the failure mode at the integration point. (b) Explain why the absence of errors and the absence of load is the strongest clue you have. (c) Name the two settings you would check first, and say which one you'd bet on.

A nightly job holds a pooled TCP connection to a partner's service. It runs fine all week. Every Monday at 06:10 it hangs for about thirty minutes, then throws. No code has changed. The partner insists their service was up the whole time — and their logs prove it. (a) State your hypothesis in one sentence. (b) Name the single packet-level observation that would confirm it. (c) Give the cheapest fix and say why the two obvious fixes — validating the connection before use, or closing connections older than an hour — both fail.

Your recommendations service runs twelve instances behind a load balancer. At 14:02 one instance stops responding. By 14:09 all twelve are gone, and the gaps between failures got noticeably shorter each time. Upstream, the product-page service is also down — its own CPU and memory look normal, but its thread count is pinned at maximum. (a) Name the two distinct antipatterns at work. (b) Say which one travelled sideways and which travelled upward, and what carried each. (c) Give the one pattern that would have stopped each, and say why swapping the two patterns would not have worked.

A team speeds up a slow partner API by subclassing an existing in-memory cache and overriding get() to fetch on a miss. The parent's get() is synchronized . Code review passes, load tests pass. In production, when the partner API stops responding, the entire service hangs — even though only 2% of traffic touches that feature. (a) Explain the mechanism in one sentence. (b) Name the object-oriented principle violated and the one-line reason the compiler didn't stop it. (c) Give one code-level fix and one architectural fix, and say which one you'd ship tonight.

Your team ships pagination by storing each user's full search-result set in the session. Load tests at 500 concurrent users pass comfortably. Two months after launch the fleet starts running out of memory every afternoon, and the crashes across instances get closer together each time. (a) Name the three antipatterns chained together here and the order they fire in. (b) Give the cheapest code change that stops today's bleeding. (c) Give the change that eliminates the whole class of problem, and say what it costs you.

An ops team sets the config-management agent to pull on the hour and the cache-warming job to run at 00:00. Separately, they add an autoscaler that reacts to one-second CPU samples, while a new instance takes five minutes to become useful. (a) Name the two failure modes you now expect. (b) Say which one is a control-plane problem and what makes it different in kind from the other. (c) Give one specific safeguard for each, and name the pattern each safeguard belongs to.

A checkout service calls three things: (i) an inventory service your own team owns, (ii) a third-party tax API with a hard rate limit and no health endpoint, (iii) an internal fraud model that is slow but usually correct. Overnight, traffic doubles because of a marketing email nobody warned you about. (a) Choose one primary pattern for each of the three dependencies and justify each in one line. (b) Name the pattern you'd apply to your own inbound traffic, and say why it is not the same one you used for (ii) even though both are about “too much load”. (c) Name the conversation you should have had last week and with whom.

A colleague proposes: “Let's wrap every outbound call in a circuit breaker, and store the breaker state in a shared Redis so all instances agree on when it's open. And let's trip it at ten failures total.” (a) Give the two objections — one about where the state lives , one about how you count . (b) Name the mechanism you'd propose for counting instead, and describe it in one sentence. (c) The team's real requirement is “we want to see globally when a provider is sick.” Satisfy that requirement without sharing breaker state.
Why is it called the number-one killer?
